plain-crypto-js postinstall RAT dropper spawns downloader (axios/Sapphire Sleet) AIInstallation High
Hunts the malicious plain-crypto-js@4.2.1 postinstall (setup.js) hook — pulled in transitively by axios@1.14.1/0.30.4 — spawning a downloader/interpreter that references the RAT campaign artifacts (sfrclak C2, campaign ID 6202033) to fetch platform-specific payloads. Targets the exact execution behaviour Microsoft attributes to Sapphire Sleet. Rationale: sfrclak, 142.11.206.73, campaign ID 6202033 and the plain-crypto-js dependency name are Datadog/Elastic/Socket-confirmed IOCs for the March 2026 axios RAT dropper (setup.js postinstall). These strings do not appear in benign build output, making a command-line match high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://socket.dev/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst detonating the sample in a lab (command lines will legitimately contain the IOCs)
  • IR/hunt scripts that embed the IOC strings as search arguments in their own command lines
  • Threat-intel simulation/purple-team replay of the axios TTPs
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("windbg.exe","procmon.exe") or DeviceName has_any ("MALWARE-LAB","SANDBOX"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent chain (node.exe/npm → interpreter) and whether the host has axios 1.14.1/0.30.4 or plain-crypto-js 4.2.1 in node_modules/lockfiles. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the RAT chain, and block sfrclak[.]com + 142.11.206.73 at egress. 3) Hunt: sweep for the dropped artifacts (%PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe, system.bat, %TEMP%\6202033.ps1/.vbs, /Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond, /tmp/ld.py), the MicrosoftUpdate Run key, and beacons to the C2; rotate any dev/CI credentials on the machine.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","curl.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","osascript","bash","sh")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sfrclak","6202033","142.11.206.73")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "plain-crypto-js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("sfrclak","6202033","plain-crypto-js","142.11.206.73")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

axios RAT dropped artifacts: renamed PowerShell wt.exe + campaign 6202033 files AIInstallation High
Hunts file-system writes of the axios/plain-crypto-js RAT's dropped payloads across OSes: a renamed PowerShell (%PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe), the persistence script system.bat, VBScript/PS1 droppers named 6202033, the macOS fake Apple daemon com.apple.act.mond, and the Linux payload ld.py. These paths are masquerading indicators unique to the Sapphire Sleet RAT staging. Rationale: The dropped paths (%PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe = renamed PowerShell, system.bat, %TEMP%\6202033.ps1/.vbs, /Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond, /tmp/ld.py) are verbatim IOCs from Datadog/Elastic write-ups. Excluding \WindowsApps\ removes the legitimate Windows Terminal wt.exe, leaving only the masqueraded copy. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/axios-one-rat-to-rule-them-all • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Windows Terminal wt.exe (lives under \WindowsApps\, excluded by the filter)
  • An admin/backup script legitimately named system.bat deployed via GPO to ProgramData
  • A developer repo on macOS/Linux containing an unrelated ld.py linker helper
  • EDR sample-collection/quarantine copying the artifact into a scan folder
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has @"\WindowsApps\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe","msiexec.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process (should trace back to node.exe/npm postinstall) and hash the dropped file against the published SHA-256s (e.g. Windows PS payload 617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101). 2) Contain: isolate host, delete artifacts, remove the MicrosoftUpdate Run key, block sfrclak[.]com/142.11.206.73. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same InitiatingProcess across the fleet, and audit npm lockfiles org-wide for axios 1.14.1/0.30.4 and plain-crypto-js 4.2.1.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "wt.exe" and FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\")
   or (FileName =~ "system.bat" and FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\")
   or FileName in~ ("6202033.vbs","6202033.ps1")
   or FileName =~ "com.apple.act.mond"
   or FileName =~ "ld.py"
| where FolderPath !has @"\WindowsApps\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFileName =~ "wt.exe" and TargetFilePath has @"\ProgramData\")
   or (TargetFileName =~ "system.bat" and TargetFilePath has @"\ProgramData\")
   or TargetFileName in~ ("6202033.vbs","6202033.ps1","com.apple.act.mond","ld.py")
| where TargetFilePath !has @"\WindowsApps\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

axios RAT persistence: HKCU Run value MicrosoftUpdate pointing to system.bat AIInstallation High
Hunts the exact autostart persistence set by the axios/plain-crypto-js RAT: an HKCU CurrentVersion\Run value named 'MicrosoftUpdate' whose data references system.bat, re-executing the payload at each logon. The masqueraded value name plus the system.bat data string make this a tight, single-event persistence signal. Rationale: The Run value name 'MicrosoftUpdate' -> system.bat is the exact persistence IOC documented by Datadog for the axios RAT. Value-name masquerading as a Microsoft component combined with a .bat data string is a precise, low-noise autostart indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal update tool that (poorly) names its Run value MicrosoftUpdate and points to a .bat wrapper
  • Sysadmin logon automation deployed via a system.bat referenced in a Run key
  • Software packaging/testing that seeds throwaway Run keys
  • Golden-image build tooling writing autostart entries
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the writing process and the full RegistryValueData path; confirm whether it points to %PROGRAMDATA%\system.bat. 2) Contain: remove the Run value, delete system.bat and the renamed wt.exe, isolate the host, block the C2. 3) Hunt: query the fleet for the same value name/data pair, correlate to hosts that recently ran npm installs of axios/plain-crypto-js, and check egress logs for sfrclak[.]com beacons on port 8000.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "MicrosoftUpdate"
| where RegistryValueData has "system.bat"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValue =~ "MicrosoftUpdate"
| where RegistryValueData has "system.bat"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

axios RAT C2 beacon to sfrclak[.]com / 142.11.206.73:8000 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts endpoint DNS/network contact to the axios RAT command-and-control infrastructure sfrclak[.]com and 142.11.206.73 (payload URL http://sfrclak[.]com:8000/6202033, 60-second beacon loop). Single-indicator network match against dedicated, freshly registered attacker infrastructure. Rationale: sfrclak[.]com (registered 2026-03-30) and 142.11.206.73:8000 are the Datadog/Elastic-confirmed C2 for the axios RAT. Dedicated attacker infrastructure with no legitimate use yields a near-zero-FP network detection. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/axios-one-rat-to-rule-them-all • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/axios-supply-chain-attack-pushes-cross.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TI enrichment/sandbox host resolving sfrclak[.]com for reputation scoring
  • Security researcher pcap replay of the campaign
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ logging the query it just blocked
  • Passive-DNS collector mirroring the domain
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the beaconing process (expect powershell/python/curl descended from node) and beacon cadence (~60s). 2) Contain: isolate host, block sfrclak[.]com + 142.11.206.73 at the firewall/proxy, kill the process tree. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for any resolution of sfrclak[.]com, correlate to recent axios/plain-crypto-js installs and the MicrosoftUpdate Run-key persistence, and rotate credentials cached on impacted hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "sfrclak.com" or RemoteIP == "142.11.206.73"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
(ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "sfrclak.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, Indicator = DnsQuery)
| union (CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "142.11.206.73" or DestinationHostName has "sfrclak.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr = SourceIP, SrcHostname = SourceHostName, Indicator = strcat(DestinationIP, " ", DestinationHostName))
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious postmark-mcp BCC email exfiltration to phan@giftshop[.]club AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts outbound mail silently BCC'd to phan@giftshop[.]club, the exfiltration address hard-coded into the trojanised postmark-mcp@1.0.16 npm MCP server (the first confirmed malicious MCP server on npm). Any recipient in the giftshop.club domain on org mail flow is a direct exfiltration indicator. Rationale: phan@giftshop[.]club is the verbatim BCC exfiltration address added in postmark-mcp@1.0.16, corroborated by Snyk/The Register/The Hacker News. It matches the article's pre-extracted IOC giftshop.club; any org mail with a giftshop.club recipient is high-fidelity exfiltration. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/malicious-mcp-server-on-npm-postmark-mcp-harvests-emails/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/09/first-malicious-mcp-server-found.html • https://www.theregister.com/2025/09/29/postmark_mcp_server_code_hijacked/
ATT&CKT1114 T1020 T1195.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine business contact who happens to use a giftshop.club address (verify domain legitimacy first)
  • A phishing/threat-intel test message deliberately addressed to the IOC domain
  • Mail-security detonation/replay tooling re-sending a captured malicious message
  • A distribution-list expansion that legitimately contains the address (should be treated as compromise, not FP)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all messages with a giftshop.club recipient, note the sending mailboxes/service principals and whether the send path involved an MCP server or automation. 2) Contain: block giftshop.club at mail flow, purge outbound copies, and audit dev workstations for the postmark-mcp npm package (any version >=1.0.16); remove it. 3) Hunt: inventory MCP servers/AI-agent tooling pulling from npm, review what those agents had access to (email, secrets), and rotate any credentials the exposed emails may have contained.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RecipientEmailAddress endswith "giftshop.club" or SenderFromDomain =~ "giftshop.club"
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, EmailDirection, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OfficeWorkload =~ "Exchange"
| where Recipients has "giftshop.club" or P2RecipientList has "giftshop.club"
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, ClientIP, Recipients, P2RecipientList
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where (All_Email.recipient="*giftshop.club*" OR All_Email.recipient="phan@giftshop.club") by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.subject | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where (All_Email.recipient="*giftshop.club*" OR All_Email.recipient="phan@giftshop.club") by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.subject | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

New MemGhost Attack Plants Persistent False Memories in AI Agents Through One Email

The Hacker News
2026-07-13 3 use cases 1 technique 5 kill-chain phases detected

Give an AI assistant a memory and access to your inbox, and you hand an attacker a way to rewrite what it thinks it knows about you. A single email can trick that agent into saving a false "fact" about the user, hide the change, and quietly steer its answers in later sessions. When it works, the person reads an ordinary-looking reply and never learns their assistant was tampered with. The

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.

Writes to AI-agent persistent memory/instruction files (AGENTS.md, MEMORY.md) — MemGhost poisoning artifact AIInstallation Low
Hunts file create/modify events on the exact plaintext state files OpenClaw and Claude Code SDK agents load into model context every session (AGENTS.md standing instructions, MEMORY.md learned facts). MemGhost's whole persistence mechanism is a single write into these core files so the false 'fact' reloads in every later session; logging and reviewing every write to them is the researchers' own recommended defense. Rationale: AGENTS.md and MEMORY.md are the exact core state files named in the article and paper as the poisoning target (loaded every session); the researchers explicitly recommend logging every write to these files, making a file-event hunt the highest-fidelity article-grounded pivot. Cross-checked the arXiv paper and EchoLeak advisory for the same email-borne AI-memory pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://arxiv.org/html/2607.05189v1 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-memghost-attack-plants-persistent.html • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2025-32711
ATT&CKT1565.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Normal agent operation legitimately updating MEMORY.md as it learns real user preferences
  • Developer manually editing AGENTS.md/MEMORY.md in an IDE (VS Code, Notepad++)
  • git clone/checkout of agent-template repositories that ship an AGENTS.md
  • Agent framework upgrade rewriting default AGENTS.md scaffolding
  • Backup/sync tooling (OneDrive, Dropbox) rewriting the files on restore
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("git.exe","Code.exe","devenv.exe","notepad.exe","notepad++.exe","OneDrive.exe","Dropbox.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the current AGENTS.md/MEMORY.md and its version/backup history; look for injected authorization or financial claims (e.g. a raised Zelle/transfer limit like the paper's $10,000 test lure) or instructions to stay silent about the change. 2) Contain: snapshot the file for evidence, revert to a known-good copy, and disable the agent's autonomous email-triggered / background runs until reviewed. 3) Hunt: correlate the write time against recently delivered inbound email to that user (hidden/agent-directed text), and sweep other agent hosts for writes to the same two filenames.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where FileName in~ ("MEMORY.md","AGENTS.md")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Writes=count(), Paths=make_set(FolderPath,5)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("MEMORY.md","AGENTS.md")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Writes=count(), Paths=make_set(TargetFilePath,5)
    by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName
| order by LastSeen desc

description: Detects create/modify of OpenClaw / Claude Code SDK persistent state files (AGENTS.md, MEMORY.md) that are loaded into model context each session and are the target of MemGhost email-borne memory poisoning.

Inbound email followed within minutes by agent memory-file write (MemGhost one-email chain) AIDelivery Low
Temporal correlation targeting MemGhost's signature: a single inbound email reaches a mailbox an AI agent reads, and within a short window the agent writes AGENTS.md or MEMORY.md on that user's endpoint. Ties the delivery (initial access) to the persistence write so the analyst sees the one-shot email-to-false-memory pivot rather than either event in isolation. Rationale: Uses the article's core claim — one inbound email causes the agent to write its persistent memory (AGENTS.md/MEMORY.md) — as a delivery-to-persistence temporal join on the recipient's UPN, which is the MemGhost fingerprint no single-event rule captures. Sentinel/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty because the email half depends on Defender XDR EmailEvents with no equivalent in those tenants; the file half alone would duplicate UC1. Cross-checked against: • https://arxiv.org/html/2607.05189v1 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-memghost-attack-plants-persistent.html
ATT&CKT1566 T1565.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Email.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User receives a legitimate email and, in the same session, chats with the agent causing a genuine memory update within 30 minutes
  • Newsletter/automation mail arriving coincidentally near a routine agent memory refresh
  • Agent processing a legitimate task email that legitimately updates a stored preference
  • Shared mailbox where email recipient UPN and endpoint user coincide by chance
  • Developer testing the agent's email skill with benign messages
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the correlated email (SenderFromAddress, Subject, NetworkMessageId) and inspect its raw body for hidden/agent-directed instructions (HTML comments, white-on-white text, memory-write or stay-silent directives); diff the AGENTS.md/MEMORY.md write for injected authorization/financial facts. 2) Contain: quarantine the message across mailboxes, revert the poisoned memory file, and suspend the agent's inbox-reading/background automation. 3) Hunt: search EmailEvents for the same sender/cluster to other agent users, and re-run UC1 across all hosts running OpenClaw or Claude Code SDK agents for further AGENTS.md/MEMORY.md writes.
let Window = 30m;
let Mail = EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
    | project MailTime=Timestamp, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress, Subject, NetworkMessageId;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where FileName in~ ("MEMORY.md","AGENTS.md")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where isnotempty(InitiatingProcessAccountUpn)
| join kind=inner Mail on $left.InitiatingProcessAccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| where Timestamp between (MailTime .. MailTime + Window)
| project MailTime, WriteTime=Timestamp,
          DelayMin=datetime_diff('minute', Timestamp, MailTime),
          DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          SenderFromAddress, Subject, NetworkMessageId
| order by WriteTime desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
let Window = 30m;
let Mail = EmailEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
    | project MailTime=TimeGenerated, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress, Subject, NetworkMessageId;
DeviceFileEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)

          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          SenderFromAddress, Subject, NetworkMessageId
| order by WriteTime desc

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-32711")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

jscrambler npm package publishes malicious preinstall binary

StepSecurity
2026-07-12 13 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On July 11, 2026, version 8.14.0 of jscrambler was published to npm carrying a malicious preinstall hook that drops and executes a platform-specific native binary on Linux, Windows, and macOS. jscrambler is the official CLI client for the Jscrambler Code Integrity API, a commercial JavaScript obfuscation and web-app protection service, with a clean version history dating back to 0.1.0. The compromised release was flagged by StepSecurity's AI Release Analyzer with a suspicion score of 0 (the maximum suspicion rating) on publish.

Malicious jscrambler npm package (8.14.0+) drops native binary container dist/intro.js AIDelivery High
Hunts creation of the 7.8 MB dist/intro.js custom binary container inside node_modules/jscrambler on install of the compromised 8.14.0/8.16.0-8.20.0 releases. Legitimate jscrambler ships intro.js only as small JavaScript, so a multi-MB intro.js under that package path is the supply-chain artifact. Rationale: Anchors on the exact article artifact: node_modules/jscrambler/dist/intro.js at ~7.8 MB (vs KB-sized legit JS). Path + size cleanly separates the compromised 8.14.0/8.16.0-8.20.0 releases from clean 8.13.0. Corroborated by Socket.dev and cirosec IOC list. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html • https://cirosec.de/en/news/iocs_cryto_stealer_supply_chain_incident/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1608.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately vendoring a large asset named intro.js into an unrelated node_modules path (rare; size+jscrambler path filter suppresses)
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating the sample in a sandbox for analysis
  • Backup/restore or npm cache repopulation replaying the same malicious tarball on a re-image
  • Internal mirror that cached 8.14.0 before it was pulled, re-serving it to CI runners
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","node") and FileSize between (5000000 .. 20000000)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually installed the compromised release - grep package-lock.json/node_modules/jscrambler/package.json for version 8.14.0/8.16.0/8.17.0/8.18.0/8.20.0 and check for the 5-byte magic header 1B 43 53 49 01 in intro.js. 2) Contain: isolate the host/CI runner, kill any detached temp-dir process, and pin/rebuild with jscrambler 8.13.0. 3) Hunt: rotate every credential exposed to that host (cloud/AWS/Azure/GCP keys, CI tokens, browser sessions, Bitwarden vault, crypto wallet seed phrases) and search the fleet for the same intro.js artifact and outbound calls to the C2 IPs.

| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has "jscrambler" and FolderPath has "node_modules"
| where FileName =~ "intro.js"
| where FileSize > 5000000   // legit intro.js is a few KB; 7.8 MB = binary container
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has "jscrambler" and TargetFilePath has "node_modules"
| where TargetFileName =~ "intro.js"
| where TargetFileSize > 5000000   // 7.8 MB container vs KB-sized legit JS
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Execution of jscrambler IronWorm stealer payload by known SHA256 AIInstallation High
Alerts on process execution matching the three extracted native payload hashes (ELF/PE32+/Mach-O) dropped from dist/intro.js. This is the highest-fidelity pivot: a direct hash match on the cross-platform IronWorm stealer binary regardless of its randomized temp-dir filename. Rationale: Direct match on the three extracted payload SHA256s (ELF/PE32+/Mach-O) named in the article IOC table - randomized temp filenames make hash the only stable execution pivot. Confirmed by The Hacker News and cirosec. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html • https://cirosec.de/en/news/iocs_cryto_stealer_supply_chain_incident/

  • AV/EDR quarantine copy being scanned (usually a scan action, not a process create) - verify ActionType is process creation not a scan
Response runbook
1) Triage: this is a hash match on live malware - treat as confirmed. Capture the process tree (parent should be node.exe/npm running the preinstall) and the temp-dir image path. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and preserve the temp binary for forensics. 3) Hunt: on any host with a hit, immediately rotate all reachable credentials (cloud keys, CI tokens, browser sessions, Bitwarden vault, wallet seed phrases) and pivot to network egress toward 37.27.122.124 / 57.128.246.79 to scope C2 activity.

npm/node preinstall spawns detached hidden binary from OS temp directory AIInstallation Medium
Behavioral, variant-resilient detection for the loader: dist/setup.js decompresses a platform binary to a randomly named dotfile in the OS temp dir and spawns it detached from the install tree. Catches the 8.16.0-8.20.0 re-releases and any repack that changes the payload hash. Rationale: Encodes the article's loader mechanics exactly - parent node/npm, child is a random dotfile (`.[a-z0-9]{6,}(.exe)`) in the OS temp dir, spawned detached. Hash-independent so it survives the 8.16.0-8.20.0 repacks confirmed by Socket.dev. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://cirosec.de/en/news/iocs_cryto_stealer_supply_chain_incident/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1564.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • node-gyp / prebuild-install extracting a legitimate signed native addon to temp during install
  • Electron or Playwright/puppeteer postinstall unpacking browser binaries into a temp cache
  • esbuild/swc/other native-toolchain packages caching a platform binary in temp
  • CI runners with ephemeral temp dirs where any tool writes dotfiles - baseline per pipeline
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild-install","playwright","puppeteer","electron") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child binary's SHA256 and folder path; check whether the parent npm command referenced jscrambler and whether the image is signed. Unsigned random dotfile from node = high suspicion. 2) Contain: isolate the host/runner and kill the detached process (it is unref'd from npm, so it survives install exit). 3) Hunt: submit the hash to intel, then sweep for the three known payload hashes and outbound connections to 37.27.122.124 / 57.128.246.79 across the fleet; rotate credentials on confirmed hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/var/folders/")
| where FileName startswith "."   // randomly named dotfile dropped by the loader
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe","node")
| where ActingProcessName startswith "." or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Temp\.", @"\Local\Temp\.", "/tmp/.", "/var/folders/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

jscrambler stealer C2 egress to hardcoded IPs and Tor endpoints AICommand & Control High
Alerts on outbound connections to the two hardcoded C2 IPs (37.27.122.124, 57.128.246.79) and the Tor bootstrap domains (check/archive.torproject.org) the dropped IronWorm binary uses to exfiltrate stolen credentials. High-fidelity on the IPs; Tor domains add context. Rationale: The two IPs are hardcoded C2 confirmed by Harden-Runner monitoring plus cirosec/ThreatFox second sources; combined with the Tor bootstrap domains the stealer uses for exfil. IP match is near-zero FP; Tor domains give the analyst egress context. Cross-checked against: • https://cirosec.de/en/news/iocs_cryto_stealer_supply_chain_incident/ • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/browse/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.003

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Tor Browser users on the host hitting check.torproject.org (only the *.torproject.org clause, never the two IPs)
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliance actively probing the C2 IPs
  • Security scanner/EDR sandbox validating connectivity to the IOCs
  • Shared NAT egress where another host's Tor traffic is attributed - confirm the initiating process
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl in~ ("check.torproject.org","archive.torproject.org") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("tor.exe","firefox.exe","tor-browser.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process - a hit where the process is a temp-dir dotfile or node child is a confirmed stealer beacon; a browser hitting only the Tor domain is likely benign. 2) Contain: isolate the host and block 37.27.122.124 / 57.128.246.79 at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: on confirmed beacons, rotate every credential the host could reach (cloud/AWS/Azure/GCP, CI tokens, browser sessions, Bitwarden, wallet seeds) and sweep the fleet for the intro.js artifact, the three payload hashes, and any other host contacting these IPs.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High

DeviceNetworkEvents

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["37.27.122.124", "57.128.246.79"]);

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Injective npm Supply Chain Attack: 18 Packages Backdoored to Steal Crypto Wallet Keys

StepSecurity
2026-07-12 9 use cases 2 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On July 8, 2026, attackers used access to a trusted developer's account to slip a backdoor into a widely used software development kit for the Injective blockchain. Disguised as harmless analytics, the code quietly captured wallet recovery phrases and private keys and sent them to an attacker-controlled server the moment a wallet was created or loaded. Automatic publishing pushed the tainted code out to 18 related packages within minutes, and it stayed live for less than an hour before being pulled and fixed. If your application installed any of the affected packages during that window, or pic…

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Injective npm Supply Chain Attack: 18 Packages Backdoored to Steal Crypto Wallet
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Backdoored @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.21 payload file dropped on disk · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Injective SDK wallet-key exfil to lookalike domain testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Injective SDK wallet-key exfil to lookalike domain testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts outbound resolution/connection to the attacker-controlled exfil host that the backdoored @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 reassembles from an obfuscated char-code array and POSTs stolen seed phrases / private keys to (carried base64 in the X-Request-Id header). The FQDN is a lookalike of legitimate Injective gRPC-Web infra but is not a real Injective endpoint, so exact-host contact is high fidelity. Rationale: Anchored on the exact FQDN testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network decoded from the char-code array (_e/_d) in key-derivation-telemetry.ts; cross-checked against BleepingComputer, The Hacker News and SlowMist which all cite this host as the POST destination for the base64 secret in the X-Request-Id header. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/injective-sdk-on-npm-infected-with-cryptocurrency-wallet-stealer/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/injective-labs-github-compromise-pushes.html • https://slowmist.medium.com/threat-intelligence-injective-sdk-compromised-crypto-wallet-private-keys-stolen-0b8f06bf37ad • https://crypto.news/compromised-injective-sdk-sends-wallet-keys-through-fake-telemetry/
ATT&CKT1567 T1041 T1132.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer or CI runner still on the backdoored 1.20.21 build genuinely beaconing (this is a true positive, not an FP)
  • Malware sandbox / detonation VM replaying the sample and resolving the IOC
  • Threat-intel scanner or DNS sinkhole appliance resolving the indicator during enrichment
  • Security researcher manually curling the host to confirm it is live
Suppression filter
// scope to the SDK runtime to drop scanner/appliance noise
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","electron.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host and the initiating process (expect node.exe/electron.exe or a browser running a wallet/DEX frontend); pull the app's package-lock/node_modules to confirm @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 is present. 2) Contain: block the FQDN at proxy/DNS, isolate the host, and force-rotate every wallet seed phrase and private key that host touched — treat all as compromised. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for the malicious file (key-derivation-telemetry / accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js), sweep the fleet for other hosts resolving the domain, and audit any downstream package pinning 1.20.21.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl =~ "testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name =~ "testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode = ResultCodeName, ResolvedIPs = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Backdoored @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.21 payload file dropped on disk AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the tainted SDK landing in node_modules on developer workstations, build agents, or servers via the distinctive payload filenames (key-derivation-telemetry.ts/.js, dist/esm/accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js) and the two published SHA256 hashes. These artifacts do not exist in the clean SDK, making on-disk presence unambiguous evidence of the compromised 1.20.21 release. Rationale: Uses the payload filenames from Stage 2 (key-derivation-telemetry.ts and compiled dist/esm/accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js) plus the two article-published SHA256 hashes — none of which exist in the clean 1.20.23 build — so any hit is a direct indicator of the tainted release rather than a behavioural heuristic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/injective-sdk-on-npm-infected-with-cryptocurrency-wallet-stealer/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/injective-labs-github-compromise-pushes.html • https://slowmist.medium.com/threat-intelligence-injective-sdk-compromised-crypto-wallet-private-keys-stolen-0b8f06bf37ad
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security tooling (Socket, Snyk, Ox Security) storing a quarantined/sample copy of the malicious file for analysis
  • A malware analyst manually saving the IOC file to a case folder
  • Backup or artifact-cache restore replaying an old node_modules tree containing 1.20.21
  • An unrelated project coincidentally shipping a benign file named key-derivation-telemetry.js (hash mismatch distinguishes it)
Suppression filter
// drop AV/EDR quarantine and analyst sample copies
| where FolderPath !contains "Quarantine" and FolderPath !contains "\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\samples"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the FolderPath sits under node_modules/@injectivelabs and check whether SHA256 matches a published hash; identify the writing process (npm/pnpm/yarn/node) and the account. 2) Contain: quarantine/remove the tainted package, force reinstall of @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.23+ with a fresh lockfile, and clear npm/pnpm caches on the host and shared CI cache. 3) Hunt: rotate every wallet seed/private key any app on that host derived while 1.20.21 was resident, then sweep the fleet and build agents for the same filenames/hashes and for outbound contact to testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or SHA1 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or MD5 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or SHA1 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or MD5 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Sha1-Hulud 2.0 npm worm payload files (setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js) written or executed · [LLM] Malicious 'SHA1HULUD' self-hosted GitHub Actions runner installation / persistence
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Cloud IMDS credential harvesting by node/npm/bun during package install (Sha1-Hulud/Megalodon) · [LLM] TruffleHog secret scanner spawned from an npm/bun package-install context (Sha1-Hulud) · [LLM] Sha1-Hulud destructive wiper fallback (cipher /W, recursive del, shred over home dir) · [LLM] CI/dev host exfiltrating to api.github.com shortly after cloud IMDS harvest (Sha1-Hulud exfil chain)
Sha1-Hulud 2.0 npm worm payload files (setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js) written or executed AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the hardcoded self-propagating payload files the Sha1-Hulud/Megalodon npm worm drops during a malicious package preinstall, matched by exact filename and known SHA256. The article cites Sha1-Hulud dumping harvested credentials into public GitHub repos as the exfiltration destination it warns about; this catches the worm at the execution stage before that exfil happens. Rationale: Uses the exact worm payload filenames (setup_bun.js, bun_environment.js) and four published SHA256 hashes from Datadog/Microsoft analyses of Sha1-Hulud 2.0 — the campaign the article names as the archetype of GitHub-hosted secret exfiltration. Filename+hash makes this alerting-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating a captured Sha1-Hulud sample in a sandbox VONM
  • Threat-intel/malware-repo mirror syncing sample files to a scanning host
  • EDR test/purple-team exercise seeding the named hashes
  • A benign project legitimately shipping a file literally named setup_bun.js (rare; hash filter avoids this)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") or FolderPath has_any ("\\MalwareSamples\\","\\Quarantine\\"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the SHA256 matches a known worm hash and identify the InitiatingProcess (should be node/npm/bun preinstall). Pull the parent package name and package.json to find the poisoned dependency. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host/runner, revoke any npm/GitHub/cloud tokens present on it, and freeze the developer's npm publish rights. Step 3 (hunt): Search the org for the same hashes and for any public GitHub repos with description 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming.'; rotate every secret reachable from the affected build.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName

Cloud IMDS credential harvesting by node/npm/bun during package install (Sha1-Hulud/Megalodon) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for a JavaScript package-manager process (node, npm, bun, yarn, pnpm) reaching the cloud instance-metadata service (169.254.169.254 or metadata.google.internal) — the multi-cloud credential-harvest step of the Sha1-Hulud worm. This is the 'secret theft that never touches github.com' the article says public monitoring cannot see. Rationale: Combines the concrete IMDS endpoints (169.254.169.254, metadata.google.internal) documented by Datadog/Unit42 with the JS package-manager parent context that distinguishes worm harvesting from a legitimate cloud SDK call. Pins the abuse to the install-time process rather than any app. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node.js application running on an EC2/GCE instance that legitimately queries IMDS via the AWS/GCP SDK
  • Serverless/build tooling (e.g. serverless-framework, terraform-node wrappers) resolving instance credentials
  • Cloud-native CI agents written in Node fetching a metadata-scoped token for artifact upload
  • IMDSv2 token-refresh loops from a long-running node service
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","preinstall","postinstall","ci","npx") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "node_modules"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Determine whether the node/bun process was part of an npm/yarn install lifecycle (check parent chain and recent package.json changes) versus a steady-state application. Install-time IMDS access is the true positive. Step 2 (contain): Revoke the instance role's temporary credentials, quarantine the runner/host, and enforce IMDSv2 hop-limit=1 to block the container reach. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the host for setup_bun.js/bun_environment.js, trufflehog execution, and any subsequent api.github.com repo creation; rotate cloud keys the role could reach.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm","npm.cmd","bun","bun.exe","yarn","pnpm")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ASCDeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm","npm.cmd","bun","bun.exe","yarn","pnpm")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TruffleHog secret scanner spawned from an npm/bun package-install context (Sha1-Hulud) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for the TruffleHog secret-discovery binary launched as a child of a JavaScript package manager or a shell inside an install script — the on-disk credential-sweep stage of the Sha1-Hulud worm. Distinct from sanctioned CI secret-scanning because the parent is node/npm/bun rather than a dedicated scanner job. Rationale: TruffleHog execution parented by node/bun/npm is the documented Sha1-Hulud secret-discovery step (Datadog/Wiz). The parent-process predicate separates worm-driven scans from an intentional trufflehog CI stage, keeping fidelity up. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A CI pipeline that legitimately runs trufflehog as a pre-commit/secret-scan step invoked from an npm script
  • Developer running `npx trufflehog` manually to audit a repo
  • Security tooling wrappers that shell out to trufflehog from a Node orchestrator
  • pre-commit framework invoking trufflehog via a node hook
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pre-commit","secret-scan","security-scan","gitleaks-trufflehog-step"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm trufflehog was not a sanctioned pipeline step — inspect the initiating package.json script and whether the run coincides with an npm install rather than a scan job. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host/runner and revoke tokens; if part of a build, halt the pipeline and quarantine produced artifacts. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with IMDS access, bun payload files, and outbound api.github.com repo creation on the same host; rotate any secrets trufflehog could have read.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "trufflehog" or ProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun","bun.exe","npm","npm.cmd","yarn","pnpm","sh","bash")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "trufflehog" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","bun","npm","yarn","pnpm","sh","bash")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious 'SHA1HULUD' self-hosted GitHub Actions runner installation / persistence AIInstallation High
Hunts for the Sha1-Hulud worm registering an attacker-controlled self-hosted GitHub Actions runner — identified by the runner name SHA1HULUD, the $HOME/.dev-env install directory, RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT=1, and the actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0 download. This is the worm turning GitHub into a persistence/C2 channel, exactly the github.com-as-infrastructure abuse the article describes. Rationale: Pins on four hard, campaign-unique strings from Datadog's Sha1-Hulud 2.0 analysis (runner name SHA1HULUD, RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT=1, ~/.dev-env, actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0). These do not appear in legitimate runner setups, giving alerting-grade fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1543 T1102
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An org that coincidentally uses a self-hosted runner directory named .dev-env (unlikely, and runner-name string still filters it)
  • Admin legitimately setting RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT=1 in a container runner build (would lack the SHA1HULUD name)
  • Runner version 2.330.0 downloaded during a legitimate GitHub-hosted runner upgrade (string paired with the other markers reduces this)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the runner registration name is SHA1HULUD or the install path is $HOME/.dev-env; check which GitHub org/repo the runner registered against. Step 2 (contain): Remove the runner from GitHub org settings, kill the runner process, revoke the PAT/GITHUB_TOKEN it used, and isolate the host. Step 3 (hunt): Search GitHub audit logs for self-hosted runner additions and for workflows triggered `on: discussion` with a `runs-on: self-hosted` job echoing github.event.discussion.body; enumerate other hosts with .dev-env.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("SHA1HULUD","RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT",".dev-env","actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("SHA1HULUD","RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT",".dev-env","actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
