Sha1-Hulud destructive wiper fallback (cipher /W, recursive del, shred over home dir) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for the Sha1-Hulud worm's destructive fallback that fires when it cannot authenticate/propagate: on Windows `del /F /Q /S %USERPROFILE%` plus `cipher /W:%USERPROFILE%`, and on Linux `find $HOME ... | xargs shred -uvz`. High-impact, low-frequency behaviour that turns a supply-chain compromise into data destruction. Rationale: Encodes the exact destructive commands Datadog documented for Sha1-Hulud's failure path (`cipher /W:%USERPROFILE%`, `del /F /Q /S %USERPROFILE%*`, `find $HOME ... shred -uvz`). cipher /W over a user profile and shred over $HOME are near-zero in normal ops, making impact-stage alerting reliable. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1485 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin/GPO running `cipher /W:` to wipe free space during decommissioning (usually not scoped to %USERPROFILE% and not spawned by node)
  • Backup or forensics tooling using shred for secure deletion of scratch data
  • A cleanup script using recursive del on a temp path (USERPROFILE token filter reduces this)
  • Disk-sanitisation compliance jobs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun","bun.exe","sh","bash","cmd.exe","powershell.exe") or FileName =~ "cipher.exe"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the parent process — a wipe parented by node/bun/sh during an npm install is the true positive; capture the exact target path. Step 2 (contain): Immediately isolate the host from the network to stop further destruction and preserve volume shadow copies/backups; snapshot the disk. Step 3 (hunt): Confirm the Sha1-Hulud chain (bun payloads, trufflehog, IMDS, SHA1HULUD runner) on the host and across the fleet; initiate restore-from-backup and org-wide secret rotation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "cipher.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/W:")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "shred" and ProcessCommandLine has "-uvz")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has_all ("del","/F","/Q","/S") and ProcessCommandLine has "USERPROFILE")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (ActingProcessName has "cipher.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "/W:")
    or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "shred" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "-uvz")
    or (ActingProcessCommandLine has_all ("del","/F","/Q","/S") and ActingProcessCommandLine has "USERPROFILE")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CI/dev host exfiltrating to api.github.com shortly after cloud IMDS harvest (Sha1-Hulud exfil chain) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates a package-manager process reaching cloud IMDS with the same host contacting api.github.com/github.com within 30 minutes — the Sha1-Hulud pattern of harvesting cloud secrets then pushing them into a newly created public GitHub repo. This directly targets the 'close the exfiltration gap' thesis of the article: catching secrets leaving CI toward github.com, not after they surface. Rationale: Chains the two documented Sha1-Hulud network behaviours (IMDS credential harvest → push to a new github.com repo) on the same host within a tight window, which is far more specific than either signal alone and maps precisely to the article's exfiltration-to-github concern. Time-window correlation makes it a hunt, not an alert. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1567.001 T1552.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node app on a cloud VM that reads IMDS and also pushes to GitHub (e.g. a release bot / GitOps agent) within the window
  • CI runner that legitimately fetches instance credentials then interacts with the GitHub API for status checks
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style automation touching both IMDS and github.com
  • Container build that queries metadata for a token and pushes an image manifest referencing github.com
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","preinstall","postinstall") or RemoteUrl has "api.github.com"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the github.com interaction — was a NEW repo created (check GitHub audit log for repo.create with an 18-char hex name or description 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming.')? Confirm the IMDS call was install-time. Step 2 (contain): Delete the attacker repo, revoke the developer's GitHub token and the instance role credentials, and isolate the host/runner. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep for bun payload files, trufflehog, and the SHA1HULUD runner on the host; enumerate all public repos org-wide matching the campaign description and rotate every exposed secret.

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-30066")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-30066")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Internal reconnaissance via Advanced IP Scanner (Gentlemen discovery) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] GentleKiller BYOVD — vulnerable/malicious driver load for EDR kill · [LLM] Windows event log clearing via wevtutil (Gentlemen anti-forensics) · [LLM] Exposure to Gentlemen-exploited edge/CVE initial-access vulnerabilities · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — No Manners Here: The Ruthless Rise of The Gentlemen Ransomware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] The Gentlemen RaaS scheduled task persistence (gentlemen* / WindowsConnSvc) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] SystemBC SOCKS5 C2 — svchost32.exe masquerade to Gentlemen C2 IPs · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] The Gentlemen ransomware impact — .axfsmg encryption, ransom note & GentlemenCollection staging · [LLM] SMB self-propagation fan-out from a single internal host (Gentlemen lateral movement) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
The Gentlemen RaaS scheduled task persistence (gentlemen* / WindowsConnSvc) AIInstallation High
Hunts creation/execution of scheduled tasks named 'gentlemen*' (per Unit 42) or 'WindowsConnSvc' (the 2-minute SYSTEM task Huntress tied to SystemBC beaconing). Article-specific because both task-name strings are unique to this operator. Rationale: Uses two operator-unique scheduled-task strings — 'gentlemen*' (Unit 42 recommendation) and 'WindowsConnSvc' (Huntress DFIR) — both far too specific to appear in benign task naming. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://www.huntress.com/blog/the-gentlemen-ransomware-defense-evasion-ttps
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal red-team/purple-team emulating The Gentlemen TTPs
  • A legitimately named custom task coincidentally containing 'WindowsConnSvc' from a third-party connectivity agent
  • Threat-intel enrichment tools writing sample task names during detonation in a sandbox
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("redteam","pentest")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full task XML (Get-ScheduledTask / schtasks /query /xml) and the InitiatingProcess — confirm SYSTEM context and 2-minute recurrence. 2) Contain: disable/delete the task, isolate the host, and capture the task action binary (often C:\Windows\Temp\svchost32.exe) for analysis. 3) Hunt: sweep the estate for the same task name, for svchost32.exe, and for beacons to 193.233.202.17/77.110.122.137/45.86.230.112.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("gentlemen","WindowsConnSvc")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("gentlemen","WindowsConnSvc")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: The Gentlemen Ransomware Scheduled Task Persistence

SystemBC SOCKS5 C2 — svchost32.exe masquerade to Gentlemen C2 IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts The Gentlemen's SystemBC proxy: the masquerading binary svchost32.exe run from C:\Windows\Temp and/or outbound connections to the confirmed C2 IPs 193.233.202.17 (port 44729), 77.110.122.137, 45.86.230.112. Article-specific via the exact IPs plus the svchost32 masquerade name. Rationale: Combines three externally-confirmed C2 IPs (Huntress/Check Point) with the svchost32.exe-from-Temp masquerade that distinguishes SystemBC from the legitimate System32 svchost.exe — both are high-fidelity, low-FP anchors. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/the-gentlemen-ransomware-now-uses-systembc-for-bot-powered-attacks/ • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/dfir-report-the-gentlemen/ • https://www.huntress.com/blog/the-gentlemen-ransomware-defense-evasion-ttps
ATT&CKT1090 T1573.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate service coincidentally reusing one of the C2 IPs after infrastructure reallocation (verify current WHOIS/ownership before dismissing)
  • A renamed monitoring agent literally named svchost.exe outside System32 (rare)
  • Threat-intel sandbox VM in the estate deliberately beaconing to these IPs for research
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process behind the connection (svchost32.exe from Temp is confirmed malicious); pull its hash and command line. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, block the three C2 IPs at egress, kill/quarantine svchost32.exe. 3) Hunt: pivot on the WindowsConnSvc scheduled task, GentleKiller driver loads, and .axfsmg files across the environment to scope the intrusion depth.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("193.233.202.17","77.110.122.137","45.86.230.112")
    or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost32.exe"
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Windows\System32" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Windows\SysWOW64")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("193.233.202.17","77.110.122.137","45.86.230.112")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceAction, RequestURL

GentleKiller BYOVD — vulnerable/malicious driver load for EDR kill AIExploitation High
Hunts The Gentlemen's GentleKiller EDR-killer loading known vulnerable drivers (ThrottleStop.sys/CVE-2025-7771 plus GentleKiller's eb.sys, nseckrnl.sys, GameDriverX64.sys, stpm_old/new.sys, dmx.sys, 360netmon_wfp.sys) or installing a 'Havoc' kernel service. Specific to the driver set catalogued by ESET/Securonix. Rationale: Matches the exact BYOVD driver filenames catalogued across ESET/Securonix/THN write-ups of GentleKiller plus the article-named ThrottleStop.sys (CVE-2025-7771) — these anti-cheat/utility drivers have no business loading on enterprise servers. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/the-gentlemen-raas-uses-gentlekiller.html • https://securityaffairs.com/193941/malware/inside-gentlekiller-the-edr-killer-powering-the-gentlemen.html
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A workstation with a genuinely installed FACEIT/Valorant anti-cheat driver (nseckrnl.sys/GameDriverX64.sys) on a developer or gaming-adjacent endpoint
  • Legitimate ThrottleStop CPU-tuning utility installed by an enthusiast on a laptop
  • Safetica/Javelin DLP genuinely deployed (stpm_*.sys) in the estate
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in (dynamic(["gaming-workstations-machine-group"])) and FolderPath !has @"\Program Files\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loading process and whether the host role should ever run anti-cheat/CPU-tuning drivers; check for a preceding svchost32.exe or ransomware activity. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the driver hash via WDAC/ASR, and confirm EDR tamper-protection status (GentleKiller targets 400+ security processes). 3) Hunt: enumerate services named 'Havoc', look for mass EDR process terminations, and scope for .axfsmg encryption downstream.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

Windows event log clearing via wevtutil (Gentlemen anti-forensics) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts execution of wevtutil to clear Security/System event logs — an explicit Unit 42 recommendation and a Gentlemen defense-evasion step. Also surfaces the native 1102 'audit log cleared' event on Sentinel. Rationale: Directly implements Unit 42's 'alert on wevtutil clearing Security/System logs' recommendation; the 'cl'/'clear-log' verb on wevtutil is rarely benign, and Sentinel adds the native 1102 signal. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://www.huntress.com/blog/the-gentlemen-ransomware-defense-evasion-ttps
ATT&CKT1070.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin manually clearing a noisy log during troubleshooting
  • Log-management/SIEM onboarding scripts that reset local logs after forwarding
  • Golden-image build pipeline clearing logs before sysprep
  • Automated software installers that clear their own application logs (less common with 'cl Security')
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("deploy.exe","sccm.exe") and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which log was cleared (Security/System are highest concern) and the parent process/account; SYSTEM or an unexpected user is suspicious. 2) Contain: preserve remaining forwarded logs, snapshot the host, and isolate if paired with any other Gentlemen indicator. 3) Hunt: because logs are now gone locally, pivot to forwarded/SIEM copies for preceding GentleKiller driver loads, svchost32.exe, and scheduled-task creation on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "wevtutil.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cl ","clear-log")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 1102 or (EventID == 4688 and NewProcessName endswith "wevtutil.exe" and CommandLine has_any ("cl ","clear-log"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, SubjectUserName, CommandLine

Internal reconnaissance via Advanced IP Scanner (Gentlemen discovery) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts execution of Advanced IP Scanner, named by Unit 42 and corroborated (Trend Micro/Huntress) as the operator's internal network mapping tool. Matches on binary name and embedded product-name metadata to survive renaming. Rationale: Advanced IP Scanner is explicitly named in the article and corroborated by Trend Micro; matching on both the binary name and the 'Advanced IP Scanner' product-metadata string catches renamed portable copies attackers drop. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/unmasking-the-gentlemen-ransomware.html
ATT&CKT1046 T1018
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT/helpdesk staff running Advanced IP Scanner for legitimate inventory
  • Network engineers troubleshooting connectivity
  • MSP tooling bundling the scanner
  • A one-off admin subnet audit
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("helpdesk-svc","netops") and DeviceName !has "JUMP"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the executing account is IT/admin and whether the host is an admin jump box; unusual users or servers running it is the signal. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, isolate host and reset the account credentials. 3) Hunt: correlate the scan window with subsequent SMB fan-out (port 445), remote-admin tool use, and GentleKiller activity to confirm active intrusion vs benign inventory.

| where FileName =~ "advanced_ip_scanner.exe" or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Advanced IP Scanner" or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "advanced_ip_scanner.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "advanced_ip_scanner.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

The Gentlemen ransomware impact — .axfsmg encryption, ransom note & GentlemenCollection staging AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the encryption/impact phase: files renamed to the .axfsmg extension, the README-GENTLEMEN.txt ransom note, and the GentlemenCollection staging directory (all confirmed by Huntress/Check Point DFIR). Directly answers the article's impact-phase gap. Rationale: Uses three externally-confirmed impact artifacts — the .axfsmg encryption extension, README-GENTLEMEN.txt note, and GentlemenCollection staging dir (Huntress/Check Point) — none of which occur benignly, giving near-zero-FP ransomware confirmation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/the-gentlemen-ransomware-defense-evasion-ttps • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/dfir-report-the-gentlemen/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/the-gentlemen-ransomware-now-uses-systembc-for-bot-powered-attacks/
ATT&CKT1486 T1074.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher detonating a Gentlemen sample in an approved lab VM within the monitored estate
  • Backup/AV quarantine copies of the ransom note preserved from a prior incident
  • Threat-hunt IOC files intentionally staged for detection testing
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "MALWARE-LAB"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm scope — count of .axfsmg files and hosts; identify the encrypting process (InitiatingProcess) and its origin. 2) Contain: immediately isolate all affected hosts, disable the responsible account, block the encryptor hash, and preserve one encrypted sample + the note for recovery/negotiation decisioning. 3) Hunt: because encryption is late-stage, work backwards — GentlemenCollection staging implies prior exfiltration, so scope SystemBC C2, data egress volume, and lateral SMB spread to identify all compromised systems before restoring backups.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".axfsmg" or FileName =~ "README-GENTLEMEN.txt" or FolderPath has @"\GentlemenCollection"
| summarize FileCount = count(), EncryptedFiles = countif(FileName endswith ".axfsmg"), RansomNotes = countif(FileName =~ "README-GENTLEMEN.txt"), StagingHits = countif(FolderPath has "GentlemenCollection"), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SampleFolder = any(FolderPath) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".axfsmg" or TargetFileName =~ "README-GENTLEMEN.txt" or TargetFilePath has "GentlemenCollection"
| summarize FileCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleFile = any(TargetFilePath) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName
| order by FirstSeen desc

Exposure to Gentlemen-exploited edge/CVE initial-access vulnerabilities AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces assets vulnerable to the specific CVEs Unit 42 says The Gentlemen exploit for initial access/privesc: CVE-2024-55591 (FortiOS/FortiProxy), CVE-2025-32433 (Erlang/OTP SSH), CVE-2025-33073 (Windows SMB Client), CVE-2025-55182 (React2Shell), CVE-2025-7771 (ThrottleStop.sys). A prioritized patch-hunt, not a behavioral alert. Rationale: Directly operationalizes Unit 42's 'immediately scope and patch' list with the five exact CVE IDs the operator is known to exploit; TVM inventory is the correct surface for pre-exploitation exposure hunting. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://www.fortiguard.com/threat-actor/6387/the-gentlemen-ransomware
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Assets flagged vulnerable but already virtually-patched via compensating controls (WAF/network ACL)
  • End-of-life network appliances TVM can only partially fingerprint (version ambiguity)
  • Devices where the CVE is present but the vulnerable service is disabled
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank the returned assets by internet exposure (edge/VPN/SMB-facing first) and severity. 2) Contain: emergency-patch or isolate internet-facing FortiOS/Erlang-SSH/React2Shell assets; for CVE-2025-33073 (SMB Client) enforce SMB signing. 3) Hunt: on any asset that was exposed, retro-hunt for prior exploitation — anomalous edge-device auth, web shells, and the downstream Gentlemen indicators (svchost32.exe, WindowsConnSvc task, GentleKiller drivers).

SMB self-propagation fan-out from a single internal host (Gentlemen lateral movement) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts one internal host opening SMB (445) sessions to many internal targets in a short window — the self-propagation behavior Unit 42 warns about and tied to CVE-2025-33073 (Windows SMB Client). Threshold-based sweep detection distinct from PsExec named-pipe rules. Rationale: Implements Unit 42's guidance to contain the SMB 'self-propagation mechanism' (CVE-2025-33073); the 25-target/10-min fan-out from a non-machine account isolates worm-like spread without duplicating PsExec/named-pipe detections. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/dfir-report-the-gentlemen/
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1210
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualls) or Advanced IP Scanner sweeping 445 legitimately
  • SCCM/Intune distribution point pushing packages to many endpoints
  • Backup agents enumerating file shares across the estate
  • A domain controller or file server with naturally high SMB fan-out
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in (dynamic(["SCCM01","BACKUP01","VULNSCAN01"])) and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("nessus.exe","advanced_ip_scanner.exe","ccmexec.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host and account; confirm whether it is a sanctioned scanner/management server (exclude those). 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, network-isolate the source host and disable the account initiating the SMB sessions. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source host for GentleKiller drivers, svchost32.exe C2, and .axfsmg encryption on the destination hosts to determine how far propagation reached.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 445 and RemoteIPType == "Private"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(RemoteIP), Targets = make_set(RemoteIP, 40), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where DistinctTargets >= 25   // one host -> 25+ internal SMB targets in 10 min = sweep / self-propagation
| order by DistinctTargets desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstPortNumber == 445
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr)
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(DstIpAddr), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DistinctTargets >= 25   // fan-out threshold for lateral SMB sweep
| order by DistinctTargets desc

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count(RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true, as=DistinctTargets))
| DistinctTargets >= 25

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent

| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| order by files desc

ImFileEvent

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

DeviceEvents

        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718"]);

[GHSA / CRITICAL] GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8: TSDProxy: Internal proxy auth token forwarded to backend services enables management API escalation

TSDProxy: Internal proxy auth token forwarded to backend services enables management API escalation

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] TSDProxy management-API token replay via CLI to loopback (x-tsdproxy-auth-token + x-tsdproxy-id) · [LLM] TSDProxy forwarded auth-token harvest via backend header-reflection endpoint (/debug/headers)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] TSDProxy management API access on loopback (/api/v1) with forged x-tsdproxy-id in proxy logs
TSDProxy management-API token replay via CLI to loopback (x-tsdproxy-auth-token + x-tsdproxy-id) AIExploitation High
Hunts the GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8 exploitation step where a compromised backend replays the stolen internal proxy token from localhost to the TSDProxy management port (127.0.0.1:8080) with an attacker-chosen x-tsdproxy-id, bypassing Tailscale auth to gain full proxy admin control. Keys on the exact header strings and management endpoint the PoC uses on the process command line. Rationale: Uses the PoC's literal strings x-tsdproxy-auth-token, x-tsdproxy-id and the 127.0.0.1:8080 /api/v1 management target from GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8 — this header pair on any command line is not legitimate TSDProxy behaviour (the proxy sets these internally, never on a CLI). Cross-checked GLAD and CVEReports write-ups of the same advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-G936-7JQJ-MWV8
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or maintainer reproducing GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8 in a lab
  • Internal pentest / purple-team validating the TSDProxy patch
  • A monitoring script that legitimately probes /api/v1 health but should never carry x-tsdproxy-auth-token (investigate if it does)
  • Automated config-management tooling that copies example curl commands from the advisory
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pentest","lab","repro") or DeviceName has_any ("lab-","test-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line and the parent process; confirm the request targeted the loopback management port (127.0.0.1:8080) and used a forged x-tsdproxy-id. Identify the initiating user/service and whether it is a proxied backend account. 2) Contain: block the offending process/account, rotate the TSDProxy per-process auth token by restarting the service, and set identityHeaders:false as interim mitigation; upgrade to >=1.4.4-0.20260603142855-434819b4421e. 3) Hunt: review /api/v1/proxies, pause/restart and webhook-trigger calls on that host, and audit all backends sharing the tsdproxy network namespace / host-network Docker containers for the harvest step (/debug/headers or token-echoing endpoints).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-auth-token"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1:8080","x-tsdproxy-id","/api/v1/")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-auth-token"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1:8080","x-tsdproxy-id","/api/v1/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName

TSDProxy management API access on loopback (/api/v1) with forged x-tsdproxy-id in proxy logs AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts server-side evidence of the same escalation: requests reaching the TSDProxy management HTTP server on 127.0.0.1:8080 for /api/v1 endpoints (e.g. /api/v1/proxies) carrying an x-tsdproxy-id claim. Because the management plane is loopback-only, TSDProxy's own access/application logs (Syslog) are the ground-truth source, not a WAF. Rationale: Targets the concrete management endpoints (/api/v1, /api/v1/proxies) and forged identity header (x-tsdproxy-id) named in GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8, scoped to the loopback management port 8080 where only TSDProxy internals should ever call — external/backend-originated /api/v1 traffic is the escalation. Defender/Falcon left empty because the traffic is loopback-only and never touches EDR network/XDR telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/ • https://almeidapaulopt.github.io/tsdproxy/docs/advanced/tailscale/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TSDProxy's own internal management calls (the legitimate identity-resolution path) if they surface in logs — baseline the expected caller
  • Local admin using the management API for legitimate start/stop/pause of proxies
  • Health-check or monitoring agent polling /api/v1 on the management port
  • Upgrade/patch verification traffic after applying the fixed version
Suppression filter
| where not (SyslogMessage has "caller=127.0.0.1" and ProcessName has "tsdproxy" and SyslogMessage has "internal")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the /api/v1 request originated from the tsdproxy process itself or from a separate/backend PID on the same host or namespace; extract the x-tsdproxy-id value used. 2) Contain: restart TSDProxy to rotate the per-process token, apply identityHeaders:false, and firewall/segment backends off 127.0.0.1:8080 (or move management off host-network). 3) Hunt: enumerate which proxies were listed/paused/restarted, check for webhook-delivery abuse (SSRF via configured webhook URLs), and pivot to the backend that could reach loopback for the token-harvest evidence.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ProcessName has "tsdproxy" or SyslogMessage has "tsdproxy"
| where SyslogMessage has "/api/v1/"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("x-tsdproxy-id","/api/v1/proxies","127.0.0.1:8080")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog @process.name:tsdproxy ("/api/v1/proxies" OR "x-tsdproxy-id")

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/api/v1/*" AND (Web.dest_port=8080 OR Web.dest="127.0.0.1")) by Web.src Web.dest Web.dest_port Web.http_method Web.url Web.status | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
TSDProxy forwarded auth-token harvest via backend header-reflection endpoint (/debug/headers) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the credential-access step of GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8 where an attacker with control of a proxied backend reads the unconditionally forwarded x-tsdproxy-auth-token out of the incoming request — the PoC does this by curling a header-reflection endpoint (/debug/headers) that echoes request headers. Surfaces processes reading such endpoints or the token string appearing in backend request-handling. Rationale: Uses the PoC's /debug/headers header-reflection endpoint and the x-tsdproxy-auth-token secret name from GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8 — a backend process reading its own reflected headers to extract that token is the harvest precursor to management-API replay. Marked Medium confidence because /debug/headers is the advisory's example endpoint, not a fixed IOC; the token-string clause anchors fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-G936-7JQJ-MWV8
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers legitimately using a /debug/headers endpoint to troubleshoot proxy header propagation
  • Application health-checks that echo request headers
  • Observability tooling capturing request metadata that includes x-tsdproxy-auth-token (this itself is a token-exposure finding worth flagging)
  • curl-based smoke tests of a newly proxied backend
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "/debug/headers" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck","readiness","liveness"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine which backend/host ran the command and whether /debug/headers (or any header-echo endpoint) actually returned x-tsdproxy-auth-token; treat any log/response containing that token as an exposed secret. 2) Contain: restart TSDProxy to rotate the token, set identityHeaders:false, and remove/disable header-reflection debug endpoints on proxied backends. 3) Hunt: on the same host/namespace look for the follow-on replay (x-tsdproxy-auth-token + x-tsdproxy-id to 127.0.0.1:8080 /api/v1 — see companion UC) and grep backend application logs for the token string to scope exposure.

| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl","wget","python","python3","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/debug/headers","x-tsdproxy-auth-token")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","python","python3")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/debug/headers","x-tsdproxy-auth-token")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SiYuan Electron client spawns command interpreter (XSS-to-RCE via child_process) AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE payoff of CVE-2026-50551/CVE-2026-44588: a stored XSS in an attribute-view cell executes in the SiYuan renderer (nodeIntegration:true) and calls require('child_process') to run native commands. A note-taking app spawning cmd/powershell/wscript is the concrete, article-specific outcome. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete RCE mechanism — Electron nodeIntegration renderer calling require('child_process') — pinned to the named parent binary SiYuan.exe. A knowledge/notes app spawning shells is near-zero baseline. Cross-checked against the SiYuan advisory, CVE-2026-39846 (same require('child_process').exec RCE pattern) and neighbor CVE-2026-44588. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-56mp-4f3v-fgj2 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-phhp-9rm9-6gr2 • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-39846/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-50551
ATT&CKT1203 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SiYuan plugins that legitimately shell out (e.g. git-sync plugins invoking git via cmd.exe)
  • SiYuan updater/installer spawning a helper via cmd during version upgrade
  • A user-configured export/pandoc pipeline that SiYuan launches through a shell
  • Admin manually launching SiYuan from a script that reparents a console child
  • Security tooling that reparents processes and mislabels SiYuan.exe as the parent
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\git.exe","pandoc","--update","siyuan-updater") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "SiYuan")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ProcessCommandLine and grandparent chain — benign hits are git/pandoc/updater with recognizable args; malicious hits show base64/IEX/download-cradle or `calc`/reconnaissance commands and correlate to a recently opened note with an attribute-view. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the SiYuan.exe process tree, and block outbound from any spawned child; preserve the offending data/storage/av/<avID>.json for analysis. 3) Hunt: enumerate the user's synced workspace peers (same account/sync target) for the same av JSON, and check DeviceNetworkEvents for the spawned child reaching external hosts. Push SiYuan >= 3.7.0.

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","calc.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound network connection from a child process of SiYuan.exe (post-RCE C2/exfil) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts C2/exfil following CVE-2026-50551 exploitation: after the SiYuan renderer's XSS runs require('child_process'), the spawned interpreter/LOLBIN beacons out to attacker infrastructure. A shell whose parent is SiYuan.exe making a public egress is a high-signal post-exploitation pivot. Rationale: Pivots on the article's RCE mechanism into the network phase: a child of the named SiYuan.exe binary reaching a public host. Scoping to InitiatingProcessParentFileName == SiYuan.exe keeps FP near zero because SiYuan's own sync traffic originates from SiYuan.exe itself, not from a spawned shell. Sentinel/Datadog left blank — the listed Sentinel tables have no per-process egress with parent context, and Sysmon EID3 carries no ParentImage, so the parent scoping can't be expressed there. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-56mp-4f3v-fgj2 • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-39846/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041

  • certutil/curl launched by SiYuan for a legitimate asset download

| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("github.com","githubusercontent.com","b3log.org","liuyun.io") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\git.exe","--update","siyuan-updater"))

1) Triage: resolve RemoteIP/RemoteUrl reputation and inspect InitiatingProcessCommandLine — download cradles, base64, or raw IP beacons are malicious; a known package/update domain is likely benign. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the SiYuan.exe child tree, and block the destination at egress. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC1 process spawns on the same host/timeframe, sweep synced workspace peers for the same data/storage/av JSON payload, and confirm SiYuan is upgraded to >= 3.7.0.

File Browser hook-auth pre-auth RCE: filebrowser spawns shell/recon commands (CVE-2026-54088) AIExploitation High
Hunts the File Browser server binary (`filebrowser`) spawning a shell or OS discovery/tooling child process. Under CVE-2026-54088 an unauthenticated attacker injects shell metacharacters into the login username/password, which `os.Expand` substitutes unsanitised into the admin's hook-auth command, causing the `filebrowser` process to execute attacker OS commands. A file server should essentially never spawn `id`/`whoami`/`curl`/`wget`, so any such child is high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the concrete vulnerable binary name `filebrowser` (parent) plus the article's PoC injection primitive (shell metacharacters `;`/`$(`/backtick and `id`/`whoami` running under the hook command). A file-server process spawning recon/OS tooling is near-zero in benign operation. Cross-checked against filebrowser.org auth docs and auth/hook.go on GitHub. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m93h-4hw7-5qcm • https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/blob/master/auth/hook.go
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1033 T1087.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin legitimately configured a hook-auth command that shells out to an external auth backend using curl/wget (e.g. validating against an LDAP/OIDC gateway)
  • Custom container entrypoint or healthcheck wrapper also named 'filebrowser' spawning /bin/sh for readiness probes
  • Ops running the filebrowser CLI (`filebrowser config`, `filebrowser users`) interactively from a shell where the parent/child order is inverted
  • Backup/maintenance scripts invoked by a filebrowser-named systemd unit that call uname/hostname
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash") and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"^\s*test\s" and not (ProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the alert — confirm InitiatingProcessFileName=='filebrowser' and inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for injected recon (id/whoami/cat /etc/passwd) or separators; correlate to the host's web/reverse-proxy logs for a POST to /api/login in the same second. 2) Contain: isolate the host, stop the filebrowser container/service, and disable hook authentication (set auth.method back to json/proxy) or patch to filebrowser v2 > 2.63.5. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for follow-on egress/reverse shells (UC2), new files under the served directory (webshell/backdoor), new cron entries or SSH authorized_keys, and any outbound connection from the filebrowser process subtree.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "filebrowser"
| where (FileName in~ ("id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","python","python3","perl","ruby","php"))
    or (FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh","ksh")
        and (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","whoami","uname","/dev/tcp/")
             or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "filebrowser" or ParentProcessName has "filebrowser"
| where (TargetProcessName has_any ("/id","/whoami","/uname","/hostname","/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/python","/perl","/ruby","/php"))
    or (TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/ash","/zsh","/ksh")
        and (TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","whoami","uname","/dev/tcp/")
             or TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File Browser hook-auth RCE follow-on: reverse shell / egress tooling under filebrowser (CVE-2026-54088) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the File Browser process subtree spawning a reverse shell or ingress/download tool after successful command injection. Distinct from the discovery UC: this targets the C2 stage where the injected command establishes an interactive shell (`bash -i`, `/dev/tcp/`, `nc -e`, `socat`, `mkfifo`) or pulls a second-stage payload (`curl`/`wget` piped to a shell) from the `filebrowser` process. Rationale: Pairs the concrete vulnerable parent binary `filebrowser` with high-specificity reverse-shell/ingress signatures (`/dev/tcp/`, `bash -i`, `nc -e`, `socat`, `curl|wget` piped to shell) from the RCE class described in the advisory. These command-line strings are near-zero-FP and map the exploit to its C2/second-stage phase. Corroborated via filebrowser.org auth docs and the GHSA advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m93h-4hw7-5qcm • https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/blob/master/auth/hook.go
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105 T1571
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit hook-auth command that uses curl/wget to POST credentials to an external authentication API
  • filebrowser sidecar/init script that pulls config or TLS certs via curl/wget at startup
  • Admin debugging the container with `docker exec` where the shell's parent resolves to filebrowser
  • Monitoring agent invoking python from within the filebrowser service context for metrics
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("https://auth.","/certs/","/token") and ProcessCommandLine !has "/dev/tcp/" and ProcessCommandLine !has "| sh" and ProcessCommandLine !has "|sh")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the child ProcessCommandLine and resolve the destination host/port (grep for the IP after /dev/tcp/ or the nc/socat/curl target); check DeviceNetworkEvents on the same host for a matching outbound public connection in the same window. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the filebrowser process/container, block the observed C2 IP/domain at the egress firewall, and rotate any credentials/secrets readable by the filebrowser service account. 3) Hunt: search for downloaded second-stage files, persistence (cron, systemd units, authorized_keys), lateral SSH from this host, and repeat the UC1 discovery query to scope earlier recon.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "filebrowser"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh","ksh","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo","socat","import socket","import pty","curl ","wget ")
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bnc(\.traditional)?\b.*\s-[ec]\b"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "filebrowser" or ParentProcessName has "filebrowser"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/ash","/zsh","/ksh","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/curl","/wget","/python","/perl")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo","socat","import socket","import pty","curl ","wget ")
    or TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bnc(\.traditional)?\b.*\s-[ec]\b"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
